unitName.zh: 整数、分数、小数放一起比

set.title: Benchmarks: whole numbers, fractions & decimals · Unit Test

questions.question: Nika wants to compare 2/3 and 3/4. She decides to rewrite both fractions with a denominator of 12. Which pair of equivalent fractions is correct?
questions.explain: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number: 2/3 × 4/4 = 8/12 and 3/4 × 3/3 = 9/12. The common trap is adding the same number to the top and the bottom (2/3 becoming 11/12), which changes the value of the fraction.

questions.question: Which one of these fractions is greater than 1/2?
questions.explain: Compare the numerator with half of the denominator: half of 9 is 4.5, and 5 is more than 4.5, so 5/9 is past the 1/2 benchmark. The trap is thinking a big denominator makes a big fraction — 4/10 and 3/8 both sit below 1/2 because their numerators are less than half their denominators.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 and is divided into 10 equal parts. Mateo puts a dot on the 3rd mark after 0. Which number is at his dot?
questions.explain: Ten equal parts means each step is one tenth, so 3 steps is 3/10 = 0.3. The common trap is calling the 3rd mark 1/3 — you only get thirds when the line from 0 to 1 is cut into 3 equal parts.

questions.question: Ava and Ben each have the same size water bottle. On the walk home Ava drank 3/4 of her bottle and Ben drank 5/8 of his. Who drank more?
options: Ben, because 5 eighths is more pieces than 3 fourths
Ava, because 3/4 is the same as 6/8, and 6/8 is more than 5/8
Ben, because 8 is a bigger denominator than 4
They drank the same, because adding 2 to the top and 4 to the bottom of 3/4 gives 5/8
questions.explain: Rename 3/4 as 6/8 so both fractions count the same size pieces, then 6 eighths beats 5 eighths. The trap is comparing the raw numbers — more pieces only means more when the pieces are the same size.

questions.question: At a craft table in Victoria, four ribbons measure 0.8 m, 3/4 m, 1/2 m and 0.65 m. Which list puts the ribbons in order from shortest to longest?
questions.explain: Put every number in the same form first: 1/2 = 0.5 and 3/4 = 0.75, so the order is 0.5, 0.65, 0.75, 0.8. The trap is sorting the decimals into one group and the fractions into another instead of placing all four on one number line.

questions.question: Four hikers each drank part of a water bottle on the trail: Leo drank 2/3, Mia drank 3/10, Sam drank 7/8, and Jia drank 4/9. Whose amount is closest to one half of a bottle?
questions.explain: Half of 9 is 4.5, so 4/9 is only a hair below 1/2, while 2/3 is about 1/6 above it and 3/10 is well below. The trap is picking a fraction that just looks small, like 3/10, instead of checking each numerator against half its denominator.

questions.question: At sports day in Kamloops, Priya jumped 1.5 m, Owen jumped 1 2/5 m and Nina jumped 1.45 m. Which list shows the three jumps from longest to shortest?
questions.explain: First change the fraction: 2/5 = 4/10 = 0.4, so Owen jumped 1.4 m; then line up the tenths, 1.50 > 1.45 > 1.40. The classic trap is thinking 1.45 is longer than 1.5 because 45 looks bigger than 5 — writing 1.5 as 1.50 stops that mistake.

questions.question: For a school bottle drive, 14 of the 21 students in Ms. Chan's class brought bottles, and 12 of the 20 students in Mr. Singh's class brought bottles. Which class had the greater fraction of students bringing bottles, and by how much?
questions.explain: Simplify first: 14/21 = 2/3 and 12/20 = 3/5, then use fifteenths — 10/15 against 9/15, so Ms. Chan's class leads by 1/15. Two traps here: comparing the head counts (14 against 12) when the classes are different sizes, and subtracting tops and bottoms straight across.
